You can use the distance formula in three dimensions: (Δs)2=(Δx)2+(Δy)2+(Δz)2,(Δs)2=(Δx)2+(Δy)2+(Δz)2, where ΔsΔs is the magnitude of the displacement. This is the generalization of the Pythagorean Theorem to three dimensions.
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 19:36:22 t V
Each of Δx,Δy,Δx,Δy, and ΔzΔz is a side length of the cube, so they're all 3m.3m. That means
Δs=√(Δx)2+(Δy)2+(Δz)2=√(3m)2+(3m)2+(3m)2=3√3m≈5.20mΔs=(Δx)2+(Δy)2+(Δz)2=(3m)2+(3m)2+(3m)2=33m≈5.20m
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 19:36:31 t V
Let's look at units for a moment.
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 19:36:35 t V
Which of these equations uses unit symbols correctly?
Δx=3Δx=3
Δx=3mΔx=3m
Δxm=3Δxm=3
Δxm=3mΔxm=3m
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 19:37:13 t V
The correct equation is Δx=3m.Δx=3m.
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 19:37:16 t V
Without any unit symbols, we'd have Δx=3,Δx=3, and the equation wouldn't say if the length is 33 meters, centimeters, feet, etc.
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 19:37:37 t V
ΔxΔx could be measured in meters, centimeters, feet, or any other unit of length (but not kilograms, which measure mass).
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 19:38:10 t V
The equation Δx=3mΔx=3m isn't telling us that ΔxΔx is a container which, when you open it up, has ‘‘3m′′‘‘3m″ inside. Instead, ΔxΔx is a physical length - however long the side of a particular room is. That length happens to be equal to the length of three meter sticks laid end-to-end, so Δx=3m.Δx=3m.
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 19:38:42 t V
A row of 300300 one-centimeter coins would have the same length, so Δx=300cm,Δx=300cm, too.
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 19:38:48 t V
All of these can be correct at the same time:
Δx=3mΔx=300cmΔx=(9+107127)feet≈9.84feetΔx=3mΔx=300cmΔx=(9+107127)feet≈9.84feet
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 19:39:22 t V
ΔxΔx doesn't have any particular units associated with it, just a particular length, so we don't write a unit symbol next to Δx.Δx.

Since we have the "opposite" and "adjacent" sides of a right triangle, we can compute the tangent of θg.θg. We can then use an inverse tangent to find θgθg itself.

Since tanθ=north componenteast component,tan⁡θ=north componenteast component, we can use θ=arctan(north componenteast component).θ=arctan(north componenteast component).
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 19:52:34 t V
Putting in the numbers, we get θplane;g=arctan(82.1m/s295.4m/s)≈15.5∘.θplane;g=arctan(82.1m/s295.4m/s)≈15.5∘.

jonjoseph 2025-06-18 20:28:50 t V
Let y0y0 be the initial height of the golf ball, and v0yv0y be the initial velocity of the golf ball in the vertical direction. The golf ball's yy position at time tt is given by y=y0+v0yt−12gt2.y=y0+v0yt−12gt2. If gg were equal to 0,0, then the golf ball would hit the (now stationary) monkey, since it's aimed straight at the monkey and it would go in a straight line in that case.
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 20:29:30 t V
Often y0=0y0=0, ground level which is why you don't see it.
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 20:30:25 t V
However, for you calculus people this is the solution to a 2nd order differential equation so we have two constants of the motion: y0y0 and v0yv0y.
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 20:31:00 t V
(Just a reminder for those that have a little background)

In that case, the yy position of the golf ball would be y=y0+v0yt.y=y0+v0yt. So we can break down the equation for the golf ball's yy position with gravity like this: y=y0+v0ytstraight line path toward monkey's starting position−12gt2amount below thaty=y0+v0yt⏟straight line path toward monkey's starting position−12gt2⏟amount below that
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 20:32:15 t V

Within projectile motion, problems about the range of a projectile are quite common. Here, we'll walk through the most basic such question as a way to see how these questions work at the fundamental level, before tackling some questions that modify the situation a little.
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 20:37:28 t V
Suppose our projectile is a ball. Let's call the initial speed of the ball v0,v0, then also use the variables gg for gravitational acceleration, tt for time, yy for vertical component of displacement, and xx for horizontal component of displacement.
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 20:37:42 t V
Remember that in projectile motion, it helps to think about the horizontal and vertical directions separately. So let's begin by thinking about the vertical direction. What happens in the vertical direction?
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 20:37:45 t V
Simple enough - the projectile goes up and comes down! Let's find the time for it to do that.
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 20:38:00 t V
We could do it with a quadratic equation. Assuming the ball starts on the ground (at height y=0y=0), the yy position at time tt is y=v0yt−12gt2,y=v0yt−12gt2, so we could set y=0y=0 and find the time for the projectile to come back to ground. What do you get when you do that?
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 20:38:48 t V
Hint: you'll have two times. Pick the right one.

sukye 2025-06-18 20:39:46 t V

We can start by dividing by tt everywhere (since we aren't interested in the height when t=0t=0) to get 0=v0y−12gtreturn.0=v0y−12gtreturn. Then we solve for tt to get treturn=2v0yg.treturn=2v0yg.
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 20:40:35 t V
The key here is that the initial height and final height are the same. Problem is a bit harder when that is not true and, in fact, 45 degrees would no longer be the answer.
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 20:41:03 t V
Remember that we just showed for the monkey problem that if θθ is measured above the horizontal, v0y=v0sinθ.v0y=v0sin⁡θ. The time in the air is treturn=2v0sinθg.treturn=2v0sin⁡θg.
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 20:41:18 t V
(This is the most-common scenario for how angles are measured. However, be aware that some problems will define angles so that the vertical direction is a cosine, or something more complicated. So always check how the angle is defined before assuming the yy direction has a factor of sinθsin⁡θ tacked on.)
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 20:41:48 t V
Let's work on the horizontal compoent.
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 20:41:57 t V
In the horizontal direction, the projectile moves at constant speed v0cosθ.v0cos⁡θ. It does this for time treturn=2v0sinθg,treturn=2v0sin⁡θg, so the total range is xrange=(v0cosθ)⋅treturn=2v20sinθcosθg.xrange=(v0cos⁡θ)⋅treturn=2v02sin⁡θcos⁡θg.

Picking your reference frame
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 20:55:10 t V
A certain pea shooter shoots a very large number of peas in two dimensions around itself. The peas are shot at equal angles of separation from each other, and all shot with an initial speed of 10m/s10m/s relative to the pea shooter. The pea shooter is set drifting across a frictionless horizontal surface. It is approaching a certain edge of the surface at a speed of 5m/s.5m/s.

The pea shooter fires the peas while in motion. What fraction of the peas fall off the edge the pea shooter is approaching? (The other edges are all very far away.)

Summary
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 21:04:12 t V
If, when we solve a physics problem, we work entirely in terms of variables, we'll get an answer in terms of variables too. This gives us extra ways to check our answer that aren't available when we work entirely with the numbers at all the intermediate stages.
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 21:04:17 t V
In two or more dimensions, we can use the Pythagorean theorem to find the magnitude of displacement. The magnitude of displacement ΔsΔs through three dimensions, x,y,x,y, and z,z, obeys Δs=√Δx2+Δy2+Δz2Δs=Δx2+Δy2+Δz2
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 21:04:20 t V
When an object's motion comes from two or more sources, we need to use vector addition to find its net motion.
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 21:04:22 t V
We often break vectors down into their components to perform vector addition.
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 21:04:26 t V
A common class of problems is those on projectile motion - motion with constant yy acceleration and no xx acceleration. In these problems, it's often helpful to consider the xx and yy motions separately.
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 21:04:29 t V
Within projectile motion, there is a sub-class of problems on the range of a projectile. This is maximum when shooting the projectile at 45∘,45∘, assuming the start and end height are the same, that gravity is uniform, and that we can ignore air resistance.
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 21:04:34 t V
We can choose any reference frame we like to solve a problem. Choosing the right frame can make the problem a bit easier.
jonjoseph 2025-06-18 21:04:53 t V
Well done. We have an impressive class! Stay safe. See you next week.
